```{r setup, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)

library(dplyr)
```

### Problem 1

Suppose you put `n` people in a room, and want to know the probability that at
least two people share a birthday. For simplicity, we'll assume there are no
leap years (i.e. there are only 365 days) and that birthdays are uniformly 
distributed over the year (which is not the case).

Write a function that, for a fixed group size, randomly draws "birthdays" for 
each person; checks whether there are duplicate birthdays in the group; and 
returns `TRUE` or `FALSE` based on the result.

Next, run this function 10,000 times for each group size between 2 and 50. For 
each group size, compute the probability that at least two people in the group
will share a birthday by averaging across 10,000 simulation runs. Make a plot
showing the probability as a function of group size, and comment on your 
results.

```{r}
n <- 20     # define test input

birthdays <- sample(1:365, size = n, replace = TRUE)     # run function code
```

```{r}
shared_birthday <- function(n) {
  birthdays <- sample(1:365, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  any(duplicated(birthdays))
}

set.seed(20)
shared_birthday(20)
```

```{r}
set.seed(123)

n_sims <- 10000
group_sizes <- 2:50

probs <- sapply(group_sizes, function(n) {
  mean(replicate(n_sims, shared_birthday(n)))
})
```

```{r}
results <- data.frame(
  group_size = group_sizes,
  probability = probs
)

head(results)
```

### Problem 2

Read in files:
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
csv_data = 
  tibble(
    files = list.files(path = "data/data/"),
    path = str_c("data/data/", files)
  ) |>
  mutate(data = map(path, read_csv)) |>
  unnest(data)
```

Tidy data:
```{r}
data_tidy =
  csv_data |>
  mutate(
    files = str_replace(files, ".csv", ""),
    exp_arm = str_sub(files, 1, 3),
    sub_ID = str_sub(files, 5,6) 
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    week_1:week_8,
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "outcome",
    names_prefix = "week_"
  ) |>
  mutate(week = as.numeric(week)) |>
  select(exp_arm, sub_ID, subject = files, week, outcome)
```


Create spaghetti plot:
```{r}
data_tidy |>
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = outcome, group = subject, color = exp_arm)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_path() +
  facet_grid(~exp_arm) +
  labs(
    title = "Observations over time by study arm",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Outcome",
    color = "Arm"
  )
```
This plot demonstrates a clear difference between the two arms in how outcomes
change over time. In the control arm, outcomes show no consistent trend. Most 
subjects fluctuate between about -1 and 4 across the 8 weeks, and the weekly 
movement appears random rather than in any discernible pattern. Lines cross
frequently, so there is little evidence that subjects stay consistently above
or below average. Subjects in the experiential arm, display a steady, roughly
linear increase. Most start between about -1 and 3.5 at week 1 and end between
about 3 and 7 at week 8. the experimental arm also spreads out over time, with 
more variability between subjects at later weeks, suggesting that individuals
respond at different rates.
